triage.name: Neurogenic bladder
triage.reason: Urinary symptoms with a clear neurologic cause; students can build the picture from history, exam and urodynamic/post-void residual testing, though it is a syndrome rather than a single disease.

age.peak: adults with neurologic disease; bimodal in younger adults with spinal cord injury and older adults with stroke or neurodegenerative disease

demographics: Occurs in both sexes; risk tracks the underlying neurologic disorder rather than sex
More common with increasing age because stroke, Parkinson disease and dementia become more prevalent
In younger adults, most often seen after spinal cord injury or with multiple sclerosis

risk_factors.text: Parkinson disease or other neurodegenerative disease
Spina bifida or other congenital spinal anomaly
Pelvic surgery or radiation that injures bladder innervation

family_history: Multiple sclerosis in a first-degree relative
Neural tube defect in a sibling or parent

chief_complaints.text: I can't tell when my bladder is full
I keep leaking urine and can't hold it
I have to strain to get any urine out
I never feel like I've emptied my bladder
I'm going to the bathroom all the time

hpi.onset: Gradual, developing over weeks to months as the underlying neurologic condition evolves; can be abrupt after spinal cord injury or stroke
hpi.duration: Chronic, present for months to years by the time it is evaluated
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive in degenerative disease; may stabilize after a fixed injury such as spinal cord injury or stroke
hpi.radiation: Usually none; pelvic or perineal discomfort may occur with retention
hpi.quality: A mix of storage symptoms (urgency, frequency, leakage) and voiding symptoms (weak stream, straining, incomplete emptying), depending on the level of the neurologic lesion
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; can range from bothersome urgency to complete urinary retention with overflow incontinence
hpi.timing: Continuous or intermittent; often worse at night and with fatigue or stress
pertinent_negatives: Flank pain or fever suggesting pyelonephritis
Known prostate enlargement or prior prostate surgery
Symptoms of a urinary tract infection at onset
Isolated nocturnal enuresis in a child without neurologic findings

atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms may be attributed to normal aging or benign prostatic hyperplasia; cognitive impairment can mask urgency and retention, and overflow incontinence may be the only sign.
Often presents with daytime wetting, recurrent urinary tract infections or new-onset nocturnal enuresis after a period of dryness, especially with spina bifida or tethered cord.
missing_classic_features: Ability to describe urgency or incomplete emptying

atypical.how_it_differs: Pregnancy can unmask or worsen neurogenic bladder symptoms; urinary frequency and leakage are common in pregnancy itself, so the neurologic history is key.
missing_classic_features: Symptoms clearly out of proportion to pregnancy alone

atypical.how_it_differs: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can cause an insensate, high-capacity bladder with silent retention and overflow, without the classic urgency and frequency.

general.moderate: Mild discomfort, may use a wheelchair or assistive device, not toxic
general.severe: Ill-appearing if retention or infection is present, may be diaphoretic or restless
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic or confused, signs of sepsis or autonomic dysreflexia

labs.caveat: Rises with high-pressure retention, recurrent infection or obstructive uropathy; a normal value does not exclude dangerous bladder pressures.
Elevated with renal impairment from chronic retention; also influenced by hydration.
Pyuria is common even without true infection in catheterized or chronically retained bladders; interpret with culture.
Positive nitrite supports a gram-negative urinary infection; negative does not exclude it.
Microscopic hematuria is common with catheter trauma or infection; persistent gross hematuria needs urologic evaluation.
Leukocytosis suggests complicating urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis rather than the neurogenic bladder itself.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or urodynamic testing.

Usually nonspecific; may show a radiopaque urinary calculus

initial.why: Screens for infection, hematuria and pyuria before any instrumentation
Confirms or excludes urinary tract infection, which commonly complicates neurogenic bladder
Assesses renal function and electrolytes in chronic retention
Rules out pregnancy before imaging or urodynamic testing

initial.test: Renal and bladder ultrasound with post-void residual
initial.why: First-line: measures residual volume and screens for hydronephrosis and stones
Bedside bladder scan quantifies incomplete emptying and guides catheterization

confirmatory.why: Defines detrusor overactivity versus underactivity, compliance and sphincter dyssynergia, and guides management

supporting.why: Monitors renal function over time in high-pressure or retained bladders
Identifies a structural cord or cauda equina cause
supporting.only_if: myelopathy, saddle findings or unexplained neurogenic bladder
focal neurologic deficits, suspected stroke or demyelination

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast
supporting.why: Defines anatomy when stone, mass or obstruction is suspected
supporting.only_if: ultrasound is nondiagnostic or obstruction is suspected

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast
not_indicated.why: Not routine; ultrasound is preferred first-line
not_indicated.only_if: ultrasound is nondiagnostic or obstruction is suspected

not_indicated.why: Not routine without neurologic red flags
not_indicated.only_if: myelopathy, saddle findings or unexplained neurogenic bladder

not_indicated.why: Not routine without central neurologic findings
not_indicated.only_if: focal neurologic deficits, suspected stroke or demyelination

not_indicated.why: Not needed unless infection or pyelonephritis is suspected
No established role in uncomplicated urinary infection
Not needed for the diagnosis of neurogenic bladder

decision_points: Check a pregnancy test before imaging or urodynamic testing in anyone who could be pregnant
Treat symptomatic urinary infection before urodynamic testing, since infection alters bladder behavior
A large post-void residual with hydronephrosis or rising creatinine suggests dangerous bladder pressures and needs prompt drainage
Saddle anesthesia, bilateral leg weakness or new retention raises concern for cauda equina syndrome and needs urgent MRI

differential.name: Cauda equina syndrome
differential.why_considered: Acute or subacute urinary retention with lower extremity and perineal neurologic findings can look like a neurogenic bladder from a spinal cause.
differential.trigger: New urinary retention with saddle anesthesia, bilateral leg weakness or fecal incontinence

history: Abrupt onset over hours to days
Saddle numbness and progressive leg weakness
exam: Reduced or absent anal sphincter tone
labs: Normal urinalysis unless there is a coincident infection
imaging: MRI lumbosacral spine showing compression of the cauda equina by disc herniation, tumor, abscess or hematoma

differential.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
differential.why_considered: Older men with incomplete emptying, weak stream, straining and nocturia can have bladder outlet obstruction rather than a neurologic bladder.

history: Symptoms of weak stream and hesitancy
exam: Enlarged, smooth prostate on digital rectal exam
Normal perineal sensation and anal sphincter tone
Normal lower extremity strength and reflexes
labs: Elevated prostate-specific antigen may be present
Normal urinalysis unless there is infection
imaging: Ultrasound showing an enlarged prostate with elevated post-void residual and possible bladder trabeculation

differential.name: Overactive bladder
differential.why_considered: Urgency, frequency and urge incontinence are the cardinal storage symptoms of both overactive bladder and neurogenic detrusor overactivity.

history: Symptoms often triggered by running water, cold or stress
No fecal incontinence or saddle numbness
exam: Normal neurologic exam including perineal sensation, anal tone and lower extremity strength
imaging: Low or normal post-void residual on bladder scan or ultrasound

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Dysuria, urgency, frequency and suprapubic discomfort are common in both urinary tract infection and neurogenic bladder, and infection frequently complicates neurogenic bladder.

imaging: Ultrasound usually normal; may show bladder wall thickening

differential.name: Bladder cancer
differential.why_considered: Gross or microscopic hematuria and irritative voiding symptoms can occur in bladder cancer and may be mistaken for neurogenic bladder symptoms.
differential.trigger: Painless gross hematuria or persistent microscopic hematuria in a patient with voiding symptoms

history: Smoking history or occupational dye exposure
exam: Possible palpable pelvic mass in advanced disease
imaging: Bladder mass on ultrasound or CT urogram
Filling defect or wall thickening on cystography

differential.name: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy
differential.why_considered: Diabetes can cause an insensate, high-capacity bladder with silent retention and overflow incontinence, mimicking a neurogenic bladder.

history: Other autonomic symptoms such as gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension or erectile dysfunction
Gradual onset of incomplete emptying without urgency
exam: Peripheral neuropathy with reduced vibration and pinprick sensation in a stocking distribution
Normal anal sphincter tone and perineal sensation
labs: Normal urinalysis unless infection is present
imaging: Large post-void residual with a smooth bladder wall on ultrasound

differential.name: Medication-induced urinary retention
differential.why_considered: Anticholinergics, opioids and alpha-agonists can cause urinary retention and overflow incontinence that resembles neurogenic bladder.

history: Recent initiation or dose increase of an anticholinergic, opioid or sympathomimetic
Temporal relationship between the medication and urinary symptoms
imaging: Elevated post-void residual that improves after stopping the offending medication

severity.mild: Storage or voiding symptoms that are bothersome but do not cause retention, upper tract changes or recurrent infection; post-void residual is small and renal function is normal.
severity.moderate: Persistent incomplete emptying with a consistently elevated post-void residual, recurrent urinary tract infections or new hydronephrosis without renal impairment.
severity.severe: High-pressure or complete retention with overflow incontinence, bilateral hydronephrosis, rising creatinine or recurrent pyelonephritis.
severity.critical: Autonomic dysreflexia with dangerous hypertension, urosepsis, or obstructive uropathy with acute kidney injury requiring emergency drainage.

red_flags.finding: Saddle anesthesia, bilateral leg weakness or new fecal incontinence
red_flags.meaning: Cauda equina syndrome until proven otherwise; needs urgent MRI and neurosurgical evaluation
Pyelonephritis or urosepsis; needs prompt antibiotics and drainage if obstructed

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe headache, hypertension, bradycardia and flushing in a patient with spinal cord injury above T6
red_flags.meaning: Autonomic dysreflexia triggered by bladder distension; a medical emergency

red_flags.finding: Anuria or rapidly rising creatinine with hydronephrosis
red_flags.meaning: Obstructive uropathy with acute kidney injury; needs urgent decompression
Possible bladder cancer or other urothelial malignancy; needs urologic evaluation

complications.name: Recurrent urinary tract infection
clues: Increased spasticity or malaise in patients with spinal cord injury

complications.name: Bladder calculi
clues: Stone seen on ultrasound or CT

complications.name: Autonomic dysreflexia
clues: Flushing and sweating above the lesion

special_populations.differences: Often presents with daytime wetting, recurrent urinary tract infections or new-onset nocturnal enuresis after a period of dryness, especially with spina bifida or tethered cord; clean intermittent catheterization is the mainstay of management.
Symptoms may be attributed to normal aging or benign prostatic hyperplasia; cognitive impairment can mask urgency and retention, and overflow incontinence may be the only sign.

Pregnancy can unmask or worsen neurogenic bladder symptoms; urinary frequency and leakage are common in pregnancy itself, so the neurologic history is key. Clean intermittent catheterization is preferred over indwelling catheters when drainage is needed.
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can cause an insensate, high-capacity bladder with silent retention and overflow, without the classic urgency and frequency.

key_questions.question: Do you have any condition that affects your nerves or spinal cord, such as a spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, stroke or Parkinson disease?
key_questions.looking_for: A known neurologic disorder that explains bladder dysfunction

key_questions.question: When did your urinary symptoms start, and did they come on suddenly or gradually?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt onset after spinal cord injury or stroke versus gradual onset with degenerative disease

key_questions.question: Can you tell when your bladder is full?
key_questions.looking_for: Impaired bladder sensation, which points to a neurologic cause

key_questions.question: Do you leak urine, and if so, is it a constant dribble or a sudden urge you cannot hold?
key_questions.looking_for: Overflow incontinence from retention versus urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity

key_questions.question: Do you have to strain to urinate, or do you feel like you never empty your bladder completely?
key_questions.looking_for: Voiding symptoms suggesting incomplete emptying or retention

key_questions.question: How often do you urinate during the day and at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequency and nocturia, which are common storage symptoms

key_questions.question: Have you had any numbness, tingling or weakness in your legs?
key_questions.looking_for: Lower extremity neurologic deficits supporting a spinal or peripheral cause

key_questions.question: Have you had any trouble controlling your bowels or any loss of bowel control?
key_questions.looking_for: Fecal incontinence or constipation suggesting shared pelvic neurologic involvement

key_questions.question: Have you had any numbness in the saddle area, or new trouble walking?
key_questions.looking_for: Saddle anesthesia or gait decline raising concern for cauda equina syndrome

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, chills or flank pain with your urinary symptoms?
key_questions.looking_for: Urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis complicating the picture

key_questions.question: Have you ever seen blood in your urine?
key_questions.looking_for: Gross hematuria, which would raise concern for bladder cancer rather than neurogenic bladder

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, especially for bladder, prostate or muscle spasms?
key_questions.looking_for: Anticholinergics, alpha-blockers, muscle relaxants or opioids that affect bladder function

key_questions.question: Do you use a catheter, and if so, how often?
key_questions.looking_for: Indwelling or intermittent catheter use, which affects infection risk and management

key_questions.question: Have you had any pelvic surgery, radiation or childbirth that could have injured the nerves to your bladder?
key_questions.looking_for: Pelvic surgery or radiation as a cause of bladder denervation

reasoning_points: Urinary storage and voiding symptoms occur in a patient with a known or suspected neurologic disorder
Impaired bladder sensation, incomplete emptying or overflow incontinence points to a neurologic cause rather than primary bladder outlet obstruction
Lower extremity weakness, sensory loss, hyperreflexia or spasticity support spinal or central nervous system involvement
Reduced perineal sensation or decreased anal sphincter tone on exam supports sacral neurologic involvement
Elevated post-void residual on bladder scan or ultrasound confirms incomplete emptying
Urodynamic testing distinguishes detrusor overactivity from underactivity and identifies sphincter dyssynergia
Urinalysis and culture exclude urinary tract infection, which commonly complicates neurogenic bladder
Cauda equina syndrome, bladder cancer and medication-induced retention are excluded as dangerous or reversible look-alikes

easy: Known spinal cord injury with a chronic indwelling catheter and recurrent urinary tract infections
Multiple sclerosis with urgency, frequency and urge incontinence plus lower extremity sensory changes
Palpable distended bladder with a large post-void residual on bladder scan
Clear temporal relationship between neurologic disease and urinary symptoms
medium: Older adult with stroke and new incontinence attributed to aging
Diabetic patient with silent retention and overflow incontinence without urgency or frequency
Patient on an anticholinergic or opioid with new retention that mimics neurogenic bladder
Overactive bladder symptoms in a patient with mild or early neurologic disease
hard: Older man with benign prostatic hyperplasia and coexisting neurologic disease, making the cause of incomplete emptying unclear
Patient with painless gross hematuria and irritative voiding symptoms raising concern for bladder cancer
New urinary retention with saddle anesthesia or bilateral leg weakness suggesting cauda equina syndrome
Child with new-onset nocturnal enuresis after a period of dryness and subtle spinal findings
Autonomic dysreflexia with severe hypertension and bradycardia in a patient with spinal cord injury above T6
